objective: By the end of this lesson you can stay found with pilotage, dead reckoning and a time log, and if you do get lost, hold heading, climb safely, find your position with landmarks, radios or GPS, and get help from ATC early.
why: Getting lost is dangerous, especially when low on fuel. Pilots who ask for help early and keep flying the airplane turn a scary moment into a non-event.

prereading.what: Pilotage, checkpoints and brackets, 'if confused, hold the heading', dead reckoning.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 16, 16-12 to 16-13

prereading.what: GPS cautions, Lost Procedures, Flight Diversion.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 16, 16-33 to 16-35

prereading.what: Situational awareness, distractions, workload and task saturation.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 2, 2-24 to 2-25

prereading.what: Ask for help early, radar help for VFR aircraft in difficulty, transponder 7700.
prereading.label: AIM 6-1-2, 6-2-1, 6-2-2

prereading.what: MAYDAY / PAN-PAN, 121.5 MHz, what to say when lost.
prereading.label: AIM 6-3-1, 6-3-2

warmup: You are on a solo cross-country. The town you expected at 10:42 never showed up, and now nothing on the ground matches your chart. What is the very first thing you do with the airplane?

key_terms.def: Navigating by looking at landmarks and checkpoints on the ground.
Navigating by math: time, airspeed, distance and direction from a known position.
Long features on each side of your course (highway, river, railroad) that tell you if you drifted too far.
The last checkpoint you positively identified, with the time you passed it.
Headings given by a radar controller to guide you. Advisory only; you still fly the airplane safely.
Direction finding: a facility locates you from your radio transmissions.
Concerned about safety; need timely but not immediate help. A potential distress.
Serious and/or imminent danger; need immediate help.
VHF emergency frequency (line of sight), guarded by DF stations, most civil towers, radar facilities and some aircraft.
Transponder emergency code. Sets off an alarm at radar control positions.

body.p: The best lost procedure is not getting lost. Pilotage means flying by landmarks and checkpoints. It is usually combined with dead reckoning and radio navigation [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

bullets: Pick checkpoints that are prominent and easy to confirm with other features: roads, rivers, railroad tracks, lakes, power lines [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Pick brackets on each side of your course (highways, rivers, railroads, mountains). Don't cross them and you can't drift far off course [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Never trust one checkpoint alone. Choose plenty. If you miss one, keep the heading and look for the next [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Sectional scale: 1 inch = 8 SM or 6.86 NM. Half an inch off the course line is 4 SM (3.43 NM) on the ground [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

callout.text: "If confused, hold the heading. If a turn is made away from the heading, it is easy to become lost." [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]

body.p: Charts are not perfect. In busy areas some small features are left off, and new roads and buildings may not be on the chart yet [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. Big, unique features beat small ones. Near a town, you may even read its name on a water tower [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].
Use radios and GPS to back up what you see outside, not replace it. Pilotage is your safeguard against disorientation if a radio fails [[1:409|PHAK 16-22]].

check.q: You miss checkpoint 2. It isn't where it should be. What do you do first?
check.a: Hold the heading and look for the next checkpoint. Turning away from the heading makes it easy to get lost [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

chunks.title: Write down the time at every checkpoint

body.p: Dead reckoning uses time, airspeed, distance and direction. Your planned groundspeed tells you when you should reach each checkpoint, and pilotage corrects the plan as you go [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]]. As the trip goes on, note headings and times and adjust heading, GS and time [[1:408|PHAK 16-21]].

head: What a written time gives you
Why it matters when lost
rows: Last known position + time
It is exactly what ATC asks for if you are lost: last known position, time, and heading since then [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].
Elapsed time since that point

Distance = groundspeed x time [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]], so you know about how far you have gone. That draws a circle on the chart where you must be; dead reckoning uses time, speed and direction from a known point [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]].
Actual vs. estimated times
A checkpoint that is late or early is your first clue the wind or heading is off [[1:408|PHAK 16-21]].

body.p: In a diversion the PHAK says the same thing: once on the new course, note the time, then figure heading, GS, arrival time and fuel [[1:422|PHAK 16-35]].

callout.text: No times on the log means no last known position. You can only guess how far you've flown, and so can the people trying to help you.

check.q: You passed a lake at 1412 and have flown heading 090 at about 100 kt GS. It is now 1424. Roughly where are you?
check.a: About 20 NM east of the lake (12 min at 100 kt = 20 NM). Time, GS and heading from a known point is dead reckoning [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: when you think you're lost

body.p: The AFH has no lost-procedure checklist. This sequence comes from the PHAK and AIM text cited on each step.

bullets: 1. Fly the airplane. Hold your heading; don't wander [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
2. Admit it early. Being doubtful about your position already puts you in at least an urgency condition [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].
3. Climb if you can't see a town or city, watching for traffic and weather. Altitude improves radio and navigation reception and radar coverage [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].
4. Look for big landmarks: towns, water tower names, highways, rivers, railroads, lakes [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]] [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
5. Use what's on board: cross radials from two or more VORs, or a panel or portable GPS to find your position and the nearest airport [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].
6. Talk to someone using frequencies on the sectional. A controller may offer radar vectors; other facilities may offer DF help [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].
7. If it gets threatening, call on 121.5 MHz and squawk 7700 [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

8. Choose a course of action and do it: continue, divert to a nearby airport, or make a precautionary landing. AFH lists "being lost" and fuel shortage as reasons for a precautionary landing [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

head: ACS skill (what you must show)
Tolerance
rows: ACS PA.VI.D.S1 Use an appropriate method to determine position.
No numeric tolerance in the ACS
ACS PA.VI.D.S2 Maintain an appropriate heading and climb as necessary.
No numeric tolerance in the ACS
ACS PA.VI.D.S3 Identify prominent landmarks.
No numeric tolerance in the ACS
ACS PA.VI.D.S4 Use navigation systems/facilities or contact an ATC facility for assistance.
No numeric tolerance in the ACS
ACS PA.VI.D.S5 Select an appropriate course of action.
No numeric tolerance in the ACS

callout.text: Steps 3 to 6 are not a strict order. Do what fits: if a big landmark is in sight, use it; if ATC is one call away, call.

check.q: Why does the PHAK tell a lost pilot to climb?
check.a: More altitude increases radio and navigation reception range and radar coverage [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

body.p: VOR and VHF radio signals are line-of-sight. Range grows with altitude. At 1,000 feet AGL, VOR reception is only about 40 to 45 miles [[1:409|PHAK 16-22]]. Too low or too far and you get a weak signal or none [[1:413|PHAK 16-26]].

bullets: Climbing helps communications, radar detection and direction-finding detection [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2]].
121.5 MHz is also line-of-sight [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

callout.text: Climb only while you can stay VFR. Many non-instrument pilots lose control when they fly into clouds or low visibility [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]. And the AIM notes unauthorized climbs under IFR conditions in controlled airspace are prohibited except under 14 CFR 91.3(b) [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2]].

check.q: At 1,000 ft AGL, about how far can you expect to receive a VOR?
check.a: About 40 to 45 miles; it increases with altitude [[1:409|PHAK 16-22]].

chunks.title: Finding position with VOR and GPS

body.p: With a VOR or ADF you can find position by plotting bearings from two or more stations [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

bullets: Tune and identify the station by its Morse code or recorded voice ID [[1:413|PHAK 16-26]].
Turn the OBS until the needle centers. With a FROM flag, the OBS shows the radial you are on [[1:410|PHAK 16-23]] [[1:411|PHAK 16-24]].
Draw that radial from the station on the chart. Do the same with a second station. You are where the lines cross [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].
A NAV warning flag means no reliable signal: you may be too far or too low [[1:410|PHAK 16-23]].

body.p: GPS (panel or portable) can show your position and the nearest airport [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. But a handheld can lose signal, sometimes with no RAIM warning, and an expired database may show waypoints that moved or no longer exist [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]].

callout.text: If GPS disagrees with your VOR, pilotage or dead reckoning, be suspicious of the GPS (especially without RAIM). Only the pilot navigates; GPS is one tool [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]].

check.q: You center the needle on VOR A with 045 FROM, and on VOR B with 300 FROM. How do you get a fix?
check.a: Draw the 045 radial out of VOR A and the 300 radial out of VOR B on the chart; you are where they cross [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]] [[1:411|PHAK 16-24]].

chunks.title: Who can help: ATC, FSS, radar and DF

body.p: Call any facility you can reach using the frequencies on the sectional [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. Help is available from radio, radar, direction finding stations and other aircraft [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

head: Help
What it does
Needs
rows: Radar vectors (radar ATC facility)
Headings to guide you [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]] [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]
Two-way radio, inside radar coverage, radar identified [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]]
Flight Service Station (FSS)
Assists lost aircraft and aircraft in emergencies; search and rescue services [[33:204|AIM 4-1-3]]
Radio contact on an FSS or RCO frequency
DF assistance
Controller asks you to hold the mic button a few seconds, maybe turn a few times, then plots your position and gives vectors to a suitable landing site [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]
Radio contact with a DF-equipped facility
Emergency frequency; guarded by DF stations, most civil towers and radar facilities, and some aircraft [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]
Line of sight

callout.text: Radar help does not authorize you to break any rule. Vectors are advisory; flying the airplane safely is still your job [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]] [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]].

body.p: Keep the controller told about the weather you are in and the weather ahead. The controller may not know whether a vector will put you in clouds [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]. If you can land safely in VFR, choose that over a vector or approach into IFR weather [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

check.q: What three things does a radar facility need before it can give a VFR pilot vectors?
check.a: You can talk to the facility, you are in radar coverage, and you can be radar identified [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]].

head: Urgency
Distress
rows: Means
Concerned about safety; need timely but not immediate help [[34:437|P/CG Urgency]]
Serious and/or imminent danger; need immediate help [[34:337|P/CG Distress]]
Say
PAN-PAN (three times) [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]
MAYDAY (three times) [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]
Priority
Over everything except distress [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]
Absolute; commands radio silence on that frequency [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]

body.p: Where to call: the frequency you are on first. If not talking to anyone, call the facility for your area. If no answer, broadcast to "Any Station" or use 121.5 MHz. If a center doesn't answer on 121.5, call the nearest tower [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

bullets: Already talking to ATC? Keep your assigned code with Mode C unless told otherwise [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].
Can't reach anyone right away? Squawk 7700 with Mode C [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. It normally sets off an alarm at all radar control positions [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]].
You may be outside radar coverage, so keep squawking 7700 and keep trying the radio [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]].

callout.text: What to say when lost (as needed, in order): MAYDAY or PAN-PAN x3, station called, call sign and type, the problem, weather, intentions and request, LAST KNOWN POSITION, TIME AND HEADING SINCE, altitude, fuel remaining in minutes, people on board [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

body.p: After contact: do what they say, cooperate, ask if unclear, and don't switch frequency unless you must [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. In an emergency needing immediate action, the PIC may deviate from Part 91 rules as needed, and may have to send a written report if the FAA asks [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]].

check.q: You are lost but have fuel and good weather. Which call fits: PAN-PAN or MAYDAY?
check.a: PAN-PAN (urgency): doubtful about position is at least an urgency condition, needing timely but not immediate help [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]] [[34:437|P/CG Urgency]].

body.p: Lost pilots go heads-down: chart, GPS, radios. That is exactly when collisions and loss of control happen. A common accident factor is a distraction that pulls the pilot's eyes off the instruments or off scanning outside [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

bullets: Task saturation: as workload rises you fixate on one item and stop seeing everything else. Then you make decisions on partial information [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].
Fix: stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Fly the airplane first, then navigate, then talk.
Fatigue, stress and work overload all cause fixation and less situational awareness [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].
Use a passenger for simple jobs like holding the chart [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

head: Collision hazard
What to do
rows: Other traffic while you climb or look down

Climb watching for traffic [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. Your eyes need 1 to 2 seconds to refocus from the panel to an aircraft 1 mile away [[16:5|AC 90-48E 8.1.4]], and avoiding a collision takes about 12.5 seconds [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]].
Blind spots
In a climb, adjust pitch to see over the nose. In cruise, make gentle shallow banks to see ahead and to the sides [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].
Near VFR waypoints, VORs and NDBs
Watch hard: GPS accuracy means fewer off-course deviations between pilots. Use ATC services and turn on landing lights [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].
Antennas and obstacles
Guy wires are almost invisible. Never get closer than 500 feet above the tallest antenna [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

callout.text: Disorientation is not only 'where am I.' Many non-instrument pilots lose control in clouds or reduced visibility [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]. Keep VFR, keep the wings level, and look outside.

check.q: How long does AC 90-48E say it takes to see, decide and get the airplane moving to avoid a collision?

chunks.title: When to ask for help or declare an emergency

body.p: The AIM is blunt: you are in at least an urgency condition the moment you become doubtful about position, fuel endurance, weather, or anything else that could affect safety. That is the time to ask for help, not after it becomes a distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Delay has caused accidents and cost lives [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

head: Situation
Good choice
rows: Unsure of position, plenty of fuel, good VFR
Hold heading, climb, use landmarks/VOR/GPS, call ATC or FSS for help [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].
Lost and the situation gets threatening
Call on 121.5 MHz and squawk 7700 [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].
Lost and low on fuel

Very dangerous [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. Plan to be on the ground before your calculated fuel time runs out or the gauge shows low [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. Consider a precautionary landing [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].
Weather closing in, non-instrument pilot
Pick the VFR option. If VFR is no longer possible, tell the controller you are not instrument rated and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

callout.text: AFH: too many precautionary-landing situations become forced landings because the pilot uses wishful thinking instead of reason [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

body.p: Once you pick an airport, divert promptly. In an emergency, don't finish every plot and calculation before turning [[1:422|PHAK 16-35]].

check.q: According to the AIM, when should you ask for help?
check.a: As soon as you become doubtful about position, fuel, weather, or anything affecting safety, before it turns into a distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

bullets: Turning around looking for a missed checkpoint instead of holding the heading [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Forcing a ground feature to 'fit' the chart. Confirm with two or more features [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
No times on the nav log, so no last known position to give ATC [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].
Waiting too long to call. Doubt about position is already an urgency [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].
Heads-down on the GPS or chart, letting heading and altitude wander and not scanning for traffic [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].
Trusting GPS blindly when it disagrees with what you see [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]].
Accepting a vector toward clouds without telling ATC the weather [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].
Spinning the transponder knob through 7500/7600/7700 by accident on a routine code change [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]].

check.q: Name two things you lose if you don't write down checkpoint times.
check.a: A last known position with time to give ATC [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]], and a dead-reckoning distance flown since that point [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]].

chunks.title: Reading the chart: landmarks and navaid boxes

body.p: To find yourself you need two kinds of clues from the chart: landmarks on the ground, and radio navaids you can tune. The legend shows how each one is drawn.

For landmarks, a small black square with a word beside it marks the exact location of something easy to see from the air, such as a substation, fort or cemetery. Dots labeled water, oil or gas are tanks. Two small towers joined by a line are a power transmission line [[2:36|Chart Users' Guide p 36]] [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p 10]].

For navaids, read the box. The type of navaid sits on the top line of the box, with its frequency, identifier and Morse code. A star before the frequency means the navaid is part time or on request. An underlined frequency has no voice. Crosshatching means the navaid is shut down, so do not trust it [[2:25|Chart Users' Guide p 25]].
A compass rose drawn around a VOR is oriented to magnetic north. A small open circle means the navaid sits on an airport [[2:25|Chart Users' Guide p 25]].

callout.text: Tune the VOR, center the needle and note the radial. Then look for two landmarks that agree with it. One clue is a guess; two clues are a fix.

scenario.title: Hazy solo cross-country, missed checkpoint
scenario.setup: You are on your solo cross-country at 3,500 feet in haze. You logged checkpoint 2, a river bridge, at 1412. Checkpoint 3, a small town, was due at 1418; it is now 1423 and you see only farmland. You turned left and right twice looking for it, and your heading has drifted. You have about 1 hour 20 minutes of fuel. The sectional shows an approach control frequency nearby and an FSS frequency on a VOR box. Haze is thicker to the west.

questions.q: What should you have done when the town did not appear at 1418?
questions.a: Hold the heading and look for the next checkpoint. Turning away from the heading makes it easy to get lost [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

questions.q: What is your last known position, and why does it matter?
questions.a: The river bridge at 1412. ATC asks a lost pilot for last known position, time, and heading since [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]; and time x GS from there tells you about how far you've gone [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]].

questions.q: You decide to climb. What hazards come with that, and how do you manage them?
questions.a: Traffic and weather. Climb watching for traffic, adjust pitch to see over the nose [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]] [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]], and don't climb into clouds or worse haze; non-instrument pilots often lose control in reduced visibility [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

questions.q: You are fumbling with the chart, GPS and radios. What is happening and what fixes it?
questions.a: Task saturation: fixating on one task and losing awareness [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Stop, think, slow down, prioritize: fly first, then navigate, then communicate [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

questions.q: Should you call ATC now, or wait until you are lower on fuel?
questions.a: Now. You are already in at least an urgency condition because you doubt your position. Ask for help before it becomes a distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

questions.q: Approach offers a vector to your destination, but it points into the thicker haze. What do you say?
questions.a: Tell the controller the weather you have and see ahead. If a VFR option exists (such as a closer airport in better weather), choose it [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

skills.do: Determine your position by pilotage, dead reckoning from your last logged checkpoint, VOR cross-radials, or GPS.
skills.practice: On every dual cross-country, have your CFI cover the GPS and ask 'where are we?' Find it with the chart and two VOR radials, then check with GPS.

skills.do: Hold a steady heading (don't wander) and climb when appropriate, staying VFR and watching for traffic.
skills.practice: When your CFI says 'you're lost,' call out 'holding heading ___' and, if needed, 'climbing to ___ for reception, clear of clouds,' while scanning.

skills.do: Pick out and name prominent landmarks (towns, highways, rivers, railroads, lakes, power lines) and match them to the chart.
skills.practice: On local flights, name three big landmarks in view and point to them on the sectional. Confirm each with a second feature.

skills.do: Use the VOR/GPS on board, or contact ATC or FSS on a sectional frequency for help, using correct phraseology.
skills.practice: Find the nearest approach control and FSS/RCO frequencies on your chart before each leg. Practice saying the lost-aircraft call (last known position, time, heading, altitude, fuel in minutes) out loud on the ground.

skills.do: Choose and explain a safe plan: continue, divert, get vectors, or land, based on fuel, weather and daylight.
skills.practice: During simulated lost drills, state your fuel in minutes and the nearest suitable airport, then commit to a plan and say why.

quiz.q: You miss an expected checkpoint. What does the PHAK advise first?
options: Turn back and fly toward the last checkpoint you positively identified
Circle over the area until you find the missed checkpoint
Descend low enough to read road signs and town names below
Hold the heading and look for the next checkpoint
quiz.why: If one checkpoint is missed, look for the next while keeping the heading; turning away makes it easy to get lost [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

quiz.q: Why does the PHAK tell a lost pilot to climb?
options: To save fuel, since the engine burns less fuel at higher altitude
To increase radio and navigation reception and radar coverage
To get above the other traffic and obstacles so you can see them better
Because 14 CFR 91.3 requires a lost pilot to climb to a safe altitude
quiz.why: An increase in altitude increases radio and navigation reception range and radar coverage [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

quiz.q: When does the AIM say an aircraft is in at least an urgency condition?
options: Only after the engine starts to run rough or loses power and you are descending
When the fuel remaining falls to the legal 30-minute reserve for day VFR flight
The moment the pilot becomes doubtful about position, fuel, weather or safety
When ATC declares the urgency condition for you after you have reported a problem
quiz.why: AIM 6-1-2 says you are in at least an urgency condition the moment you become doubtful about position, fuel endurance, weather or other safety factors [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

quiz.q: You are lost (an urgency condition). Your radio works, but you can't raise any facility. What does the AIM say to squawk?
options: 7700 with Mode C
quiz.why: If unable to immediately establish communications with an air traffic facility, squawk Code 7700 and Mode C [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. 7600 is for a loss of two-way radio capability [[34:53|AIM 6-4-2]], not for being lost.

quiz.q: What does a controller ask you to do for DF (direction finding) assistance?
options: Squawk IDENT every 30 seconds so the controller can pick you out on the scope
Switch to 243.0 MHz and make a continuous transmission until they answer you
Read back your GPS latitude and longitude every minute until they plot you
Hold the transmit button a few seconds, then release, perhaps after turns
quiz.why: The controller asks you to hold the transmit button a few seconds and release, and may ask for a few heading changes [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

quiz.q: In a lost-aircraft call, what position information does the AIM ask for if you are lost?
options: Only the nearest VOR and the distance you think you are from it
Your best guess at the nearest town and its distance from you
Departure airport, destination and your original estimated time of arrival
Last known position, time, and heading since that position
quiz.why: Give present position and heading, or if lost, last known position, time, and heading since that position [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

quiz.q: A radar controller gives you vectors. Who is responsible for flying safely and following the regulations?
options: You, the pilot; vectors are advisory
Flight Service, since they handle lost aircraft
Both share it equally once radar contact is made
The controller, once radar contact is established
quiz.why: Radar navigation guidance is advisory; responsibility for flying safely remains with the pilot, and it does not authorize violating CFRs [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

quiz.q: You are a non-instrument-rated pilot getting vectors, and VFR flight ahead is no longer possible. What does the AIM say to do?
options: Accept the vector into the clouds and trust the controller to keep you safe
Tell the controller you are not instrument rated and declare distress
Turn off the transponder, and descend to stay below the clouds on your own
Request an IFR clearance and continue on into the clouds when it is issued
quiz.why: If continued VFR is not possible, the non-instrument-rated pilot should advise the controller, state the lack of an instrument rating, and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

quiz.q: On the navaid legend, a star appears before the OAKDALE frequency. What does it mean?
options: The navaid is shut down for service
It operates part time or on request
The navaid has no voice transmitted
The navaid is located on an airport
quiz.why: The star marks a navaid that operates less than continuous or on request [[2:25|Chart Users' Guide p 25]].

quiz.q: An underlined frequency inside a navaid box means:
options: Weather is broadcast on that frequency
The frequency is kept for emergencies
The navaid is out of service now
No voice is sent on that frequency
quiz.why: The legend says an underline indicates no voice on the frequency [[2:25|Chart Users' Guide p 25]].

quiz.q: Crosshatching over the frequency in a VOR-DME box means:
options: The navaid is brand new
The navaid is on an airport
The navaid is for military use only
The navaid is shut down
quiz.why: The crosshatch indicates shutdown status [[2:25|Chart Users' Guide p 25]].

quiz.q: On the landmark legend, two small towers joined by a line mark:
options: A pipeline running above the ground
A railroad running through a pass
A power or telecommunication line
A state or county boundary line
quiz.why: That symbol is for power transmission and telecommunication lines [[2:36|Chart Users' Guide p 36]].

quiz.q: Small black dots labeled water, oil or gas are used for:
options: Wells
Tanks
Mines
Lookout towers
quiz.why: Tanks use a small dot with the type of tank beside it. Wells use an open circle [[2:36|Chart Users' Guide p 36]] [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p 10]].

quiz.q: You are lost and are studying the chart. What does 14 CFR 91.113(b) still require when weather permits?
options: Look outside only when flying under IFR
Look outside only when ATC calls out traffic
Look outside only when below 1,200 ft AGL
Keep a lookout to see and avoid other aircraft
quiz.why: [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]] requires vigilance to see and avoid other aircraft, whether VFR or IFR, when weather conditions permit.

takeaways: If confused, hold the heading; turning makes it worse [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Log the time at every checkpoint; it is your last known position [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].
Climb (staying VFR, watching traffic) for better radio, nav and radar coverage [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].
Doubt about position = urgency. Ask for help early [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].
Fly first. Vectors are advisory; you stay responsible [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].
cfi_notes: Simulate getting lost on dual cross-countries: cover the GPS, make a few turns while the student is heads-down, then ask 'where are we?'
Watch for the student turning back and forth looking for a missed checkpoint. Insist on holding heading (PHAK 16-12).
Check that the nav log has actual times filled in. Without them the student can't give a last known position.

Many instructors teach a 'Cs' memory aid (climb, communicate, comply, etc.). The FAA sources used here don't name it, but climb (PHAK 16-34, AIM 6-3-2), communicate (PHAK 16-34) and comply (AIM 6-3-2b) all appear in the text.
Common confusion: 7700 vs. keeping the assigned code. AIM 6-3-2 says keep the assigned code when already in contact with ATC; squawk 7700 when you can't establish communications right away.
Have students practice the lost-aircraft radio call out loud, including fuel in minutes, until it is smooth.
Reinforce that 'being lost' is a listed reason for a precautionary landing (AFH 18-1). Students often don't consider landing as an option.
gaps: The AFH (FAA-H-8083-3C) has no lost-procedure checklist; the step-by-step sequence is built from PHAK 16-34 and AIM 6-1-2, 6-3-2.
The ACS Skills elements for this Task give no numeric tolerances.
No source used here lists which specific facilities offer DF service today; check the Chart Supplement or ask ATC.
Aircraft-specific items (fuel burn, endurance, best climb speed, avionics operation) come from the POH/AFM and avionics guides.

cards.s: Pilotage is usually used together with dead reckoning and radio navigation.
cards.why: Yes. Pilotage can be used alone, but it is more commonly used with dead reckoning and VFR radio navigation [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

cards.s: If a checkpoint doesn't show up, circle until you find it.
cards.why: No. Look for the next checkpoint while you keep the heading. Turning away from the heading makes it easy to get lost [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

cards.s: One clear checkpoint is enough to be sure of your position.
cards.why: No. Never rely completely on any single checkpoint. Choose plenty, and pick ones you can confirm with other features [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

cards.s: A landmark 1 inch from your course line on a sectional is about 8 statute miles off course on the ground.
cards.why: Yes. The sectional scale is 1 inch = 8 SM or 6.86 NM [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

cards.s: In dead reckoning, your groundspeed tells you when you should reach each checkpoint.
cards.why: Yes. The GS sets the time to arrive at each checkpoint and the destination [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]].

cards.s: Every road and building you see from the air is shown on a current sectional.
cards.why: No. In busy areas some smaller features are left off, and new roads and structures may not appear until the next chart [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

activities.title: What is your panel telling you?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap what it means.

pairs.r: No reliable signal: too far or too low
The OBS shows the radial you are on
Where they cross is your position

pairs.l: Signal comes in, but no Morse ID
pairs.r: Station may be out of service; don't use it
Be suspicious of the GPS position
Waypoints may have moved or no longer exist

activities.title: Build the lost-aircraft call
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the parts of the call in the order the AIM prefers, then tap Check.
steps: Name of the station you are calling
Your call sign and aircraft type
Last known position, time, and heading since

activities.title: Urgency or distress?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: You need help soon, but not right this second
Has priority over every call but one kind
Serious or imminent danger; you need help now
The call commands radio silence on the frequency
Not instrument rated, and VFR flight is no longer possible

activities.title: Read the navaid boxes
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Star: part time or on request
VORTAC box with an NDB frequency
DME box with a channel number
Compass rose, oriented to magnetic north

final_quiz.q: You logged a highway bridge at 0950. You have held heading 180 at a groundspeed of about 120 knots. It is now 1005. About where are you?
options: About 15 NM south of the bridge
About 60 NM south of the bridge
About 30 NM north of the bridge
About 30 NM south of the bridge
final_quiz.why: 15 minutes at 120 knots is 30 NM (distance = GS x time) [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]]. Heading 180 is south. Time, speed and direction from a known point is dead reckoning [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]].

final_quiz.q: A lake you plan to use as a checkpoint is 1.5 inches from your course line on the sectional. About how far from your course is it on the ground?
options: About 8 SM
About 6.9 NM
About 15 SM
About 12 SM (about 10.3 NM)
final_quiz.why: The sectional scale is 1 inch = 8 SM or 6.86 NM [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. 1.5 x 8 = 12 SM, and 1.5 x 6.86 = about 10.3 NM. 8 SM and 6.9 NM would be only 1 inch.

final_quiz.q: Your course runs between an interstate highway about 5 miles north and a large river about 6 miles south. How do these features help you stay found?
options: They tell you your exact groundspeed once you fly past each of them
They replace the need for any other checkpoints or landmarks along the route
As long as you don't cross either one, you can't drift far off course
They show you where the nearest airport is, since airports sit near them
final_quiz.why: Features on each side of the course work as brackets. By not crossing them, you keep from drifting too far off course [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. You still need plenty of checkpoints.

final_quiz.q: Look at the figure. You are lost, flying low between VOR A and VOR B, and the NAV flag shows for both stations. What change would most likely let you get a fix from both?
options: Descend closer to the terrain so the VOR signals can reach your radios
Retune both nav radios to 121.5 MHz and call for help on the guard channel
Climb, staying clear of clouds, until both signals come in
Turn away from both stations and fly that heading until the flags clear
final_quiz.why: VOR signals are line-of-sight, so reception range grows with altitude [[1:409|PHAK 16-22]]. The flag means you are too far or too low [[1:410|PHAK 16-23]]. Climbing, while watching traffic and weather, increases navigation reception range [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

final_quiz.q: Lost, you tune and identify a VOR. You turn the OBS until the needle centers with 270 at the top and a FROM flag. What do you draw on the chart?
options: A line from the station out to the west, along its 270 radial
A line from the station out to the east, along its 090 radial, toward you
A line along your current heading from the position where you think you are
A circle 27 miles around the station, since 270 shows the distance
final_quiz.why: With the needle centered and FROM showing, the OBS shows the radial, the magnetic course from the station [[1:411|PHAK 16-24]]. The 270 radial runs west from the station. A radial from a second station crosses it at your position [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

final_quiz.q: Your portable GPS has no RAIM. It shows you 8 miles east of where your VOR cross-fix and a town name on a water tower both put you. What should you do?
options: Trust the GPS, since it is always more accurate than a VOR or a landmark
Split the difference between the GPS position and the position the others show
Be suspicious of the GPS and go with what the other sources agree on
Turn off the VOR and follow the GPS so you stop getting mixed signals
final_quiz.why: Without RAIM, be suspicious of a GPS position that disagrees with radio navigation, pilotage or dead reckoning [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]]. GPS is just one tool; only the pilot can navigate.

final_quiz.q: You call approach control for help finding your position. The controller says traffic is too heavy to give you vectors right now. What is true?
options: They must give vectors to any VFR pilot who asks, whatever their workload
It is the controller's call, so try another facility, such as Flight Service
You should squawk 7600 and leave the frequency since you are not being helped
You should stop asking for help and keep searching on your own until traffic clears
final_quiz.why: Traffic volume and workload can keep a controller from giving vectors, and that decision is up to the controller [[33:218|AIM 4-1-17e]]. Flight Service stations also help lost aircraft [[33:204|AIM 4-1-3]], so keep asking.

final_quiz.q: Your airplane has no transponder, and you are outside radar coverage. You reach a facility by radio. Which kind of help can still find your position?
options: Radar vectors from approach control
Squawking 7700 so radar sees you
Traffic advisories from a radar facility
Direction finding: you hold the mic button while they locate you
final_quiz.why: For DF help, the controller has you hold the transmit button a few seconds, maybe after a few turns, then plots your position from the transmissions [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. Radar vectors need radar coverage and radar identification [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]].

final_quiz.q: You are getting VFR flight following on code 4521 when you realize you are unsure of your position. What should your transponder show?
options: Change to 7600 since you are uncertain of your position and need help
Change to 7700 right away so the controller knows you are in trouble
Keep 4521 with Mode C unless ATC tells you otherwise
Change to 1200 since you are no longer receiving the service
final_quiz.why: When you are already in radio contact with ATC, keep your assigned code and Mode C unless told otherwise. Squawk 7700 when you can't establish communications right away [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

final_quiz.q: You are lost and not talking to anyone. You call the Center on 121.5 MHz and get no answer. What does the AIM suggest next?
options: Wait 30 minutes and try again
Call the nearest tower
Squawk 7500
Turn off the radio to save the battery
final_quiz.why: Center's emergency frequency coverage normally doesn't reach as far as its radar. If a center doesn't answer on 121.5 MHz, call the nearest tower [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

final_quiz.q: You are hunting for a frequency on the chart, tuning a radio, and zooming the GPS. Your heading has drifted 30 degrees and you have lost 300 feet. What is happening, and what fixes it?
options: Task saturation; stop, think, slow down, and prioritize, flying first
Hypoxia from the altitude; descend right away and take a few deep breaths
Normal workload for a lost pilot; keep going and it will settle down soon
A VOR failure; turn off all the radios and navigate by pilotage alone now
final_quiz.why: As workload rises, a pilot focuses on one item and loses awareness of the rest. The fix is to stop, think, slow down, and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Flying the airplane always comes first.

final_quiz.q: You are lost with about 20 minutes of fuel left. No airport is in sight, nobody answers your calls, and below you is a large, smooth field in good weather. What does the AFH point to?
options: Keep searching for an airport until the fuel gets very low; something will turn up
Plan a precautionary landing in the field while you still have power
Climb as high as possible to look for an airport and glide when the fuel runs out
Wait until the engine quits on its own, then pick the best field you can
final_quiz.why: Being lost and fuel shortage are both reasons for a precautionary landing, which is less hazardous than a forced landing because you have time and power [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]. Wishful thinking turns these into forced landings.

final_quiz.q: With help from ATC you find your position, and you decide to divert to an airport 12 miles away because fuel is getting low. What does the PHAK advise?
options: Turn toward the airport promptly, then note the time and work out heading, GS, arrival time, and fuel
Fly back to your last checkpoint first, then turn
Plot the full course and work out heading, GS, and fuel before turning
Hold your old heading until you can get a weather briefing
final_quiz.why: In an emergency, divert promptly. Trying to finish all plotting and math first can make things worse. Once on course, note the time and figure heading, GS, arrival time, and fuel [[1:422|PHAK 16-35]].

final_quiz.q: A compass rose around a VOR on the chart is oriented to which north?
options: True north
Grid north
Magnetic north
The north of the nearest airport runway
final_quiz.why: The legend says the compass rose is oriented to magnetic north [[2:25|Chart Users' Guide p 25]].

final_quiz.q: A small black square with the word substation beside it tells you:
options: A radio navaid that transmits voice on VHF
The exact spot of a landmark seen from the air
A restricted area that you may not enter
A highway intersection used as a checkpoint
final_quiz.why: A brief description next to a small black square marks the exact location of many landmarks easily recognized from the air [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p 10]] [[2:36|Chart Users' Guide p 36]].

final_quiz.q: You are lost in Class E below 10,000 ft MSL, and the flight visibility has dropped to 2 SM. Does 14 CFR 91.155(a) allow VFR there?
options: Yes. 1 SM is enough in Class E airspace
Yes. VFR needs 2 SM in every class of airspace
No. It needs 5 SM at every altitude in Class E
No. Class E below 10,000 ft MSL needs at least 3 SM
final_quiz.why: Class E below 10,000 ft MSL needs 3 SM flight visibility with 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 2,000 ft horizontal from clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. If it gets worse, ask for help early.
